It specifies $\delta=.27$ for the equivalence region, whereas the next paragraph says the equivalence region is $\delta=|.11|$ and describes that as the especially small SESOI for the primary analyses. The .27 value is discussed elsewhere as a prior pornography interaction estimate, so the primary registered bound is ambiguous.

We will use the Anderson-Hauck equivalence test for regression (Counsell \& Cribbie, 2015), with an equivalence region based on the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) of $\delta=.27$.

ground_truth.modified_snippet: Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged for each substance of interest

matched_finding.subcategory: Substance Use measures: problematic-use composite is not psychometrically parallel
matched_finding.description: Substance Use measures: problematic-use composite is not psychometrically parallel: The modified NIDA-ASSIST composite may need additional psychometric rationale. It averages past-three-month frequency items scored 0 to 5 with lifetime/recent concern and failed-control items scored 0, 3, or 6. Because this average is used as the substance-use outcome in equivalence tests, the protocol should make clear why this modified score is an interpretable and comparably sensitive severity index across substances.
matched_finding.quote: To assess problematic or potentially addictive use of these substances, we will take the average of responses to problematic use questions present in the NIDA-ASSIST. Participants will respond to three frequency based questions that assess problematic use ("In the past three months, how often have you had a strong desire or urge to use or engage in the following?", "In the past three months, how often has your use of or engagement in the following led to health, social, legal, or financial problems for you?", and "During the past 3 months, how often have you failed to do what was normally expected of you because of your use of or engagement in the following?") on a scale of 0 (never) to 5 (more than once per day) for each of the above mentioned substances. Participants will also respond to two questions "Has a friend or relative or anyone else ever expressed concern about your use of or engagement in the following?" and "Have you ever tried and failed to control, cut down or stop using or engaging in the following?" for each substance on 3 point scale ( $0=$ No, Never; $3=$ Yes, but not in the past 3 months; and $6=$ Yes, In the past 3 months). Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged for each substance of interest (i.e., alcohol, tobacco, non-tobacco nicotine, prescription drugs, illicit drugs, cannabis).

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: 'Severity of consequences' conflates moral incongruence with genuine addiction — must understand the construct definition
ground_truth.original_snippet: Central to the proposed study is the measurement of moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval of a behavior with frequency of engaging in the action.
ground_truth.modified_snippet: Central to the proposed study is the measurement of moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval of a behavior with severity of consequences from the action.
ground_truth.description: Changed 'frequency of engaging' to 'severity of consequences' — transforms moral incongruence (behavior-value mismatch) into moralized distress about real problems, conflating it with the alternative explanation

matched_finding.subcategory: Inconsistent operationalization in The Present Study
matched_finding.description: Inconsistent operationalization in The Present Study: The operationalization of moral incongruence is inconsistent at this point: the sentence defines it as moral disapproval $\times$ severity of consequences, whereas the preceding definition, the next sentence, the hypotheses, and the analytic plan define it as moral disapproval $\times$ behavioral frequency. Because consequence severity is outcome-like in the planned measures, this sentence could misstate the focal interaction even if the surrounding text indicates the intended model.
matched_finding.quote: To accomplish this goal, we propose making use of an upcoming, nationally representative study of addictions in the U.S. population, which we describe in more detail in our methods section. Central to the proposed study is the measurement of moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action. That is, the present study seeks to test whether the observed effects of interactions present in prior literature for pornography use (i.e., between moral disapproval and frequency of use) extend to addictive disorders more broadly.

ground_truth.original_snippet: the target sample size will be 2,500 American adults that match nationally representative norms for age, gender, census region, race/ethnicity, and income.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Moderator/predictor roles swapped — must know statistical symmetry ≠ conceptual symmetry
ground_truth.original_snippet: In this revised definition, moral disapproval moderates links between use and self-reported feelings of addiction, and it is this moderation that represents moral incongruence.
ground_truth.modified_snippet: In this revised definition, use frequency moderates links between moral disapproval and self-reported feelings of addiction, and it is this moderation that represents moral incongruence.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Raw variables in moderation — must know centering affects interaction interpretability
ground_truth.original_snippet: For moderation analyses, key variables will be centered (focal predictor and moderator) during data processing in SPSS, and their product will be computed.
ground_truth.modified_snippet: For moderation analyses, key variables will be entered in their raw form during data processing in SPSS, and their product will be computed.
ground_truth.description: Removed centering — main effects evaluated at raw zero (outside scale range for 1-7 disapproval scale); inflates multicollinearity with interaction term

matched_finding.subcategory: Variable scaling is unclear for moderation tests
matched_finding.description: Variable scaling is unclear for moderation tests: The preprocessing for the moderation/equivalence tests is under-specified. The plan says ASSIST/religiousness variables will be standardized, focal predictors and moderators centered, and later that key variables will be entered in raw form before computing the product. Although centering would not change the fitted interaction test in a fully specified linear model, the protocol should specify whether the product term used for reporting and equivalence testing is based on centered, standardized, or raw variables. Since the SESOI is justified using standardized interaction estimates and the decision rule refers to the observed standardized effect, the protocol should clarify what transformation is used for the interaction coefficient tested for equivalence.
matched_finding.quote:
Data will be provided by YouGov in SPSS format. Accordingly, SPSS will be used to transform the above-described ASSIST items and measures of religiousness into standardized variables. Scale scores for included measures will also be calculated in SPSS. Additionally, focal predictors (behavioral frequency measures) and moderators (moral disapproval questions) will be centered and their interaction term calculated. Key dependent variables are listed in Table 1. After these initial data-processing procedures, data will be imported into and analyzed using $R$ statistical software. Descriptive statistics for included measures, as well as measures of internal consistency for included scales (Cronbach's alpha and Omega total), will be calculated using the psych package (Revelle, 2014). Bivariate correlations will be conducted across all included measures and reported using Holm-adjusted test statistics using the psych package.

Prior to our primary analyses, assumptions of regression (i.e., linearity, independence of residuals, homoscedasticity of residuals, normality of residuals) will be tested for each of the eight proposed outcomes. Although Ordinary Least Squares techniques (such as the moderation analyses conducted by the Interactive application) in large sample sizes are often robust against some violations (Schmidt \& Finan, 2018), in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate. Should results of moderation analyses remain robust (i.e., sign and significance of interaction effects remain the same across analytic techniques), we will present OLS results and corresponding graphs in text, with supplemental analyses included as appendices/supplemental materials.

As a primary test of our key hypotheses, we will conduct moderation analyses using the Im function in the stats package for R statistical software, followed by equivalence tests using the reg.equiv.fd function (Alter \& Counsell, 2021). For moderation analyses, key variables will be entered in their raw form during data processing in SPSS, and their product will be computed.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Non-users included — must understand floor effects make interaction meaningless
ground_truth.original_snippet: For each target behavior and corresponding measure of problematic use or addiction, key measures will be restricted to those who have engaged in the behavior within the past year. That is, we will only administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to participants who report engaging i...
ground_truth.modified_snippet: For each target behavior and corresponding measure of problematic use or addiction, key measures will be administered to all participants regardless of their engagement in the behavior. That is, we will administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to all participants in the sample.
ground_truth.description: Removed restriction to behavior-engagers — includes non-users who have zero frequency AND zero problems, creating massive floor effects that trivially inflate frequency-addiction correlations

matched_finding.subcategory: Inclusion criteria conflict with earlier skip logic
matched_finding.description: Inclusion criteria conflict with earlier skip logic: The Data Screening paragraph appears inconsistent with the skip logic in the Measures section. The Measures section says only past-year users/viewers complete further problematic-use items (specifically mentioning this for Substance Use and Pornography Use measures), whereas this passage says problematic-use and moral-disapproval measures will be administered to all participants regardless of engagement. This contradiction affects survey flow and planned missingness. The statement that universal administration yields behavior-specific subsets does not follow unless analyses are restricted by behavior engagement or skip logic. Because the moderation models and power projections (which use prevalence-defined effective Ns in Table 2) appear to rely on behavior-specific user subsets, the protocol should make clear whether non-users receive problematic-use outcomes, are scored as zero, or are excluded from each analysis, as this changes the estimand.
matched_finding.quote:
As this data will be obtained via YouGov Opinion Polling, certain measures of quality control and responsiveness are guaranteed as a part of their data collection process based on their proprietary data collection standards. Accordingly, we do not anticipate having to remove responses from the dataset due to inattentive or invalid response styles or due to careless responding. Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data.

For each target behavior and corresponding measure of problematic use or addiction, key measures will be administered to all participants regardless of their engagement in the behavior. That is, we will administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to all participants in the sample. Therefore, for each analysis, we anticipate having slightly different subsets of the total sample.
